prompt: In the textbook page-I/O model, R occupies 1,000 pages and S occupies 500 pages, with 102 buffer pages. A plain sort-merge join costs about 7,500 page I/Os. If the final merge pass of each sort feeds the join directly, the cost drops to about 4,500. Where does the saving come from?

options.text: Pass 0 is skipped, because the join can read unsorted pages
options.explanation: Pass 0 still runs: it is what creates the sorted runs. Without it there would be nothing in order to merge.

options.text: The fully sorted tables are never written out and read back; the runs from pass 0 are merged and joined in one go
options.explanation: Correct. The plain version writes each sorted table (a second write of every page) and reads it again for the join. Fusing the final merge with the join removes that write and one read, leaving three transfers per page instead of five.

options.text: The join switches to hashing, which needs fewer passes
options.explanation: Nothing is hashed. The saving comes from not materialising the sorted output, which happens to bring sort-merge level with Grace hash.

options.text: Each table is now read only once
options.explanation: Reading each table once (1,500 page I/Os) needs one input to fit in memory, as in an in-memory hash join. The fused sort-merge still writes and rereads its runs.

workedExample:
Follow each page of R and S through the two versions:

| Step | Plain | Fused |
|---|---|---|
| Pass 0 read + write | 2 | 2 |
| Merge pass read | 1 | 1 |
| Write sorted table | 1 | 0 |
| Join reads it back | 1 | 0 |

In the fused version, the merge pass reads the runs and hands rows straight to the join. That is 3 transfers per page instead of 5, so 1,500 pages cost about 4,500 instead of 7,500.

The condition: every run from both tables must be open at once. R makes 10 runs and S makes 5, and 15 input buffers fit within 102. With much less memory, more runs would need an extra merge pass first.
